title: Random Processes
description: Ensembles and sample functions, mean and autocorrelation, wide-sense stationarity and ergodicity, with the random-phase sinusoid, binary and telegraph signals and the Poisson process.

study.title: Ensembles and sample functions
study.body: A **random process** $X(t)$ assigns a whole waveform to every outcome of an experiment. The collection of all possible waveforms is the **ensemble**; one waveform is a **sample function**, what an oscilloscope shows on a single sweep. Fixing a time $t_0$ gives a random variable $X(t_0)$: one value per sample function. Drag $t_0$ along three sample functions of $\cos(2\pi t + \Theta)$, each with its own random phase.

study.title: Mean and autocorrelation functions
study.body: Because $X(t)$ is a random variable at every $t$, it has a **mean function** $m_X(t) = E[X(t)]$, an average over the ensemble at each time. How the values at two times are related is described by the **autocorrelation** $R_X(t_1, t_2)$ and the **autocovariance** $C_X(t_1, t_2) = R_X(t_1, t_2) - m_X(t_1)\,m_X(t_2)$. The variance at time $t$ is $C_X(t, t)$.

study.title: Wide-sense stationary processes
study.body: A process is **wide-sense stationary** (WSS) if its mean is constant and its autocorrelation depends only on the time difference $\tau = t_2 - t_1$. Then $R_X(\tau)$ is even, it is largest at $\tau = 0$, and $R_X(0) = E[X^2(t)]$ is the **average power**. If samples far apart become uncorrelated (no periodic or random constant component), $R_X(\tau) \to m_X^2$ (the DC power) for large $\tau$. Strict-sense stationarity requires all statistics to be time-invariant; for Gaussian processes the two coincide.

study.title: The random-phase sinusoid
study.body: $X(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_0t + \Theta)$ with $\Theta$ uniform on $(0, 2\pi)$ models an oscillator whose phase is unknown. Averaging over $\Theta$ gives $m_X = 0$ and the autocorrelation below, so the process is WSS with average power $A^2/2$. Its autocorrelation never dies out: a periodic process stays correlated with itself forever, which is how autocorrelation reveals periodic signals buried in noise.

study.title: Random binary and telegraph signals
study.body: A **random binary wave** is ±A, constant over bit periods $T$, with independent equally likely bits and a random start time. Samples less than $T$ apart may lie in the same bit; samples further apart never do and are uncorrelated, which gives the triangle $R_X(\tau) = A^2(1 - |\tau|/T)$ for $|\tau| < T$. A **random telegraph signal** flips between ±A at random Poisson instants with rate $\alpha$: $R_X(\tau) = A^2e^{-2\alpha|\tau|}$. Both have zero mean and power $A^2$; the faster they switch, the narrower $R_X$. Drag $T$ and $\alpha$ (A = 1).

study.title: The Poisson process
study.body: The Poisson counting process $N(t)$ counts the events (packets, photons, electrons) in $(0, t]$ when they occur independently at rate $\lambda$. $N(t)$ is Poisson with mean and variance $\lambda t$; counts in non-overlapping intervals are independent (**independent increments**); and the times between events are exponential with mean $1/\lambda$. Its mean grows with $t$, so $N(t)$ is **not** stationary: $R_N(t_1, t_2) = \lambda\min(t_1, t_2) + \lambda^2t_1t_2$. Drag $\lambda$: a sample path (staircase) stays within about ±σ of the mean.

study.title: Time averages and ergodicity
study.body: In the lab we usually see **one** sample function and average over time, e.g. a DC meter computes $\langle x\rangle$. A WSS process is **ergodic** (in the mean, in power, …) if such time averages converge to the ensemble averages. The random-phase sinusoid and filtered thermal noise are ergodic: a DC meter reads $m_X$ and a true-rms meter $\sqrt{R_X(0)}$. Counterexample: $X(t) = C$, the constant but random offset of a randomly picked op amp, is stationary, yet every time average just returns that op amp's own $C$.

steps.title: Random processes
steps.body: A **random process** $X(t)$ assigns a waveform to each outcome. All possible waveforms together form the **ensemble**; each one is a **sample function**. At a fixed time $t_0$, $X(t_0)$ is a random variable: one value per sample function (here three sample functions of a sinusoid with random phase).

steps.prompt: For a fixed time $t_0$, what is $X(t_0)$?
steps.explanation: Fixing $t$ and letting the outcome vary gives one number per sample function: a **random variable**, with its own PDF, mean and variance. Fixing the outcome and letting $t$ vary gives a sample function instead.

steps.title: Mean and autocorrelation
steps.body: The **mean function** $m_X(t) = E[X(t)]$ averages over the ensemble at each time. The **autocorrelation** tells how strongly the values at two times are related; at $t_1 = t_2 = t$ it is the mean power $E[X^2(t)]$.

steps.prompt: An oscillator outputs $X(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_0t)$ with $f_0$ = {{f0|Hz}}, where the amplitude $A$ is random with mean {{mA|V}} and standard deviation {{sA|V}}.

ask.prompt: What is the mean $m_X(t)$ at $t$ = {{t1|s}}?
ask.explanation: Only $A$ is random: $m_X(t) = E[A]\cos(2\pi f_0t)$ = {{mA|V}} × cos(2π × {{f0|Hz}} × {{t1|s}}) = {{mA|V}} × {{cos(2*pi*f0*t1)}} = **{{mA*cos(2*pi*f0*t1)|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What is $R_X(t_1, t_2)$ for $t_1$ = {{t1|s}} and $t_2$ = {{t2|s}}, in V²?
ask.explanation: $R_X(t_1,t_2) = E[A^2]\cos(2\pi f_0t_1)\cos(2\pi f_0t_2)$ with $E[A^2] = \mu_A^2 + \sigma_A^2$ = {{mA^2+sA^2}} V². The cosines are {{cos(2*pi*f0*t1)}} and {{cos(2*pi*f0*t2)}}, so $R_X$ = **{{(mA^2+sA^2)*cos(2*pi*f0*t1)*cos(2*pi*f0*t2)}}** V².

steps.title: Wide-sense stationarity
steps.body:
A process is **wide-sense stationary** (WSS) if
- its mean is the same at all times, and
- its autocorrelation depends only on the time difference $\tau = t_2 - t_1$.
Then $R_X(0) = E[X^2]$ is the average power, $R_X(\tau)$ is even, and $|R_X(\tau)| \le R_X(0)$.

steps.prompt: The process $X(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_0t)$ of the previous question, with a random amplitude $A$ and no random phase, is wide-sense stationary.
steps.explanation: Its mean $E[A]\cos(2\pi f_0t)$ changes with $t$, and $R_X(t_1, t_2) = E[A^2]\cos(2\pi f_0t_1)\cos(2\pi f_0t_2)$ depends on $t_1$ and $t_2$ separately, not only on $\tau$. At every zero crossing of the cosine, all sample functions are 0 together. A random, uniformly distributed **phase** is what makes a sinusoid stationary.

steps.prompt: $X(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_0t + \Theta)$ with $A$ = {{A|V}}, $f_0$ = {{f0|Hz}} and Θ uniform on $(0, 2\pi)$. What is $R_X(\tau)$ for $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}, in V²?
Match each property of a WSS autocorrelation to its meaning
steps.explanation: $R_X(0) = E[X(t)^2]$ is the mean power. Swapping $t_1$ and $t_2$ changes nothing, so $R_X$ is even. No delayed copy can be more similar to the signal than the signal itself, so $R_X$ peaks at $\tau = 0$. WSS requires a constant mean and an autocorrelation that depends only on $\tau$.

steps.prompt: A WSS noise voltage has $R_X(\tau) = {{a}}\,e^{-{{b}}|\tau|} + {{c}}$ (in V², with τ in seconds).

ask.prompt: What is its average power (in V², i.e. W in 1 Ω)?
ask.explanation: The average power is $R_X(0)$ = {{a}} + {{c}} = **{{a+c}}** V².

ask.prompt: What is the magnitude of its mean $|m_X|$?
ask.explanation: For large τ the samples become uncorrelated and $R_X(\tau) \to m_X^2$ = {{c}} V², so $|m_X| = \sqrt{{{c}}}$ = **{{sqrt(c)|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What is its variance, in V²?
ask.explanation: $\sigma^2 = R_X(0) - m_X^2$ = ({{a}} + {{c}}) − {{c}} = **{{a}}** V²: the decaying part of $R_X$ is the autocovariance.

steps.title: The random binary wave
steps.body: A **random binary wave** holds +A or −A for each bit period $T$ (independent, equally likely bits, random start time). Two samples less than $T$ apart may fall in the same bit and then agree; samples further apart are in different bits and are uncorrelated. The result is a triangular autocorrelation.

steps.prompt: A random binary wave of ±{{A|V}} carries {{Rb/1000}} kbit/s. What is $R_X(\tau)$ for $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}, in V²?
steps.explanation: Bit period $T = 1/R_b$ = {{1/Rb|s}}, so $\tau/T$ = {{tau*Rb}}. For $|\tau| < T$, $R_X = A^2(1 - |\tau|/T)$; for $|\tau| \ge T$ the two samples always fall in different, independent bits and $R_X = 0$. Here: **{{A^2*max(0,1-tau*Rb)}}** V².

steps.title: The random telegraph signal
steps.body: A **random telegraph signal** switches between +A and −A at random instants that form a Poisson process with rate $\alpha$ (switchings per second). $X(t)X(t+\tau)$ is $+A^2$ after an even number of switchings and $-A^2$ after an odd number; averaging gives an exponentially decaying autocorrelation.

steps.prompt: A random telegraph signal switches between ±{{A|V}} at an average rate of {{al}} switchings per second.

ask.prompt: What is $R_X(\tau)$ at $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}, in V²?
What is the correlation coefficient between $X(t)$ and $X(t+\tau)$ for $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}?
ask.explanation: The mean is 0 and the variance $A^2$, so $\rho(\tau) = R_X(\tau)/A^2 = e^{-2\alpha\tau}$ = $e^{-{{2*al*tau}}}$ = **{{exp(-2*al*tau)}}**, independent of the amplitude.

steps.title: The Poisson process
steps.body: $N(t)$ counts the events in $(0, t]$ arriving at rate $\lambda$. $N(t)$ is Poisson with mean and variance $\lambda t$; counts in non-overlapping intervals are independent; the gaps between events are exponential. Because the mean grows with $t$, $N(t)$ is not stationary. (Staircase: a sample path for λ = 2 per second; dashed: the mean.)

steps.prompt: Photons reach a detector as a Poisson process at {{lam/1e6}} million per second.

ask.prompt: What is the standard deviation of the number of photons counted in {{T|s}}?
ask.explanation: The count is Poisson with mean $\lambda T$ = {{lam*T}}, and its variance equals its mean: $\sigma = \sqrt{\lambda T}$ = **{{sqrt(lam*T)}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the probability of counting no photon at all in {{T|s}}? (probability, 0–1)
ask.explanation: $P(N = 0) = e^{-\lambda T}$ = $e^{-{{lam*T}}}$ = **{{exp(-lam*T)}}**: the probability that the first interarrival time exceeds {{T|s}}.

steps.prompt: A Poisson counting process $N(t)$ has rate $\lambda$ = {{lam}} per second. Take $t_1$ = {{t1}} s and $t_2$ = {{t2}} s.

ask.prompt: What is $E[N(t_1)\,N(t_2)]$?
ask.explanation: Split $N(t_2) = N(t_1) + [N(t_2) - N(t_1)]$; the increment is independent of $N(t_1)$. So $E[N(t_1)N(t_2)] = E[N(t_1)^2] + E[N(t_1)]\,E[N(t_2) - N(t_1)]$ = $(\lambda t_1 + \lambda^2t_1^2) + \lambda t_1\cdot\lambda(t_2 - t_1) = \lambda t_1 + \lambda^2t_1t_2$ = {{lam*t1}} + {{lam^2*t1*t2}} = **{{lam*t1+lam^2*t1*t2}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the covariance of $N(t_1)$ and $N(t_2)$?
ask.explanation: $C_N(t_1,t_2) = R_N(t_1,t_2) - m(t_1)m(t_2) = \lambda\min(t_1, t_2)$ = {{lam}} × {{t1}} = **{{lam*t1}}**: only the shared interval $(0, t_1]$ contributes.

steps.prompt: The Poisson counting process $N(t)$ is wide-sense stationary.
steps.explanation: Its mean $E[N(t)] = \lambda t$ grows with time, and $R_N(t_1,t_2) = \lambda\min(t_1,t_2) + \lambda^2t_1t_2$ is not a function of $t_2 - t_1$ alone. Its **increments** over intervals of equal length do have the same distribution (stationary increments), and the derived telegraph signal is WSS.

steps.prompt: Which graph is the autocorrelation $R_X(\tau)$ of a random binary wave with bit period $T$? (Horizontal axis: τ/T from −2 to 2.)
steps.explanation: Samples less than one bit apart lie in the same bit with probability $1 - |\tau|/T$, which gives the triangle. The two-sided exponential belongs to the random telegraph signal (Poisson switching), the cosine to a random-phase sinusoid. The rectangle cannot be an autocorrelation at all: its Fourier transform, the power spectral density, would go negative.

steps.title: Time averages and ergodicity
steps.body: Measurements use one sample function and average over time. A WSS process is **ergodic** if its time averages equal the ensemble averages: then a DC meter reads $m_X$ and a true-rms meter $\sqrt{R_X(0)}$. Noise and the random-phase sinusoid are ergodic; a random but constant DC offset $X(t) = C$ is stationary but not ergodic.

steps.prompt: Every op amp in a batch has its own constant input offset voltage $C$, random from part to part with mean 0 and σ = 1 mV. Pick a part and record its offset over time: $X(t) = C$. This process is …
options: WSS but not ergodic in the mean
WSS and ergodic in the mean
ergodic in the mean but not WSS
steps.explanation: $m_X = E[C] = 0$ and $R_X(\tau) = E[C^2]$ = (1 mV)² for every τ, so it is WSS. But the time average of one sample function is just that part's own $C$, never the ensemble mean 0: it is not ergodic. Only averaging over many parts would find the mean.

steps.prompt: A signal $X(t) = B + A\cos(2\pi f_0t + \Theta)$ has $B$ = {{B|V}}, $A$ = {{A|V}} and Θ uniform on $(0, 2\pi)$. It is WSS and ergodic.

ask.prompt: What is its average power $R_X(0)$, in V²?
What does a DC voltmeter (a time average) read?
ask.explanation: Ergodic in the mean: the time average equals $m_X = B$ = **{{B|V}}**; the cosine averages to zero.

ask.prompt: What does an AC-coupled true-rms meter read?
ask.explanation: AC coupling removes $B$; the rms of the sinusoid is $A/\sqrt2$ = **{{A/sqrt(2)|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What does a DC-coupled true-rms meter read?

steps.prompt: A WSS process has $R_X(\tau) = {{a}}\,e^{-|\tau|/\tau_c} + {{c}}$ (V²), with $\tau_c$ = {{tc|s}}.

ask.prompt: What is the correlation coefficient between $X(t)$ and $X(t+\tau)$ for $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}?
ask.explanation: The constant {{c}} V² is the DC power $m_X^2$, and the variance is $R_X(0) - m_X^2$ = {{a}} V². So $\rho(\tau) = \frac{R_X(\tau) - m_X^2}{\sigma_X^2} = e^{-|\tau|/\tau_c}$ = $e^{-{{tau/tc}}}$ = **{{exp(-tau/tc)}}**.

ask.prompt: What is $R_X(\tau)$ for $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}, in V²?
ask.explanation: $R_X$ = {{a}} × $e^{-{{tau/tc}}}$ + {{c}} = **{{a*exp(-tau/tc)+c}}** V². It never drops below the DC power {{c}} V².

steps.prompt: Which function can be the autocorrelation $R_X(\tau)$ of a WSS process?
steps.explanation: $3e^{-2\tau}$ is not even (and grows without bound for $\tau < 0$). $\tau^2e^{-|\tau|}$ is 0 at $\tau = 0$ but positive elsewhere, violating $|R(\tau)| \le R(0)$. $-e^{-|\tau|}$ would give a negative power $R(0) = -1$. The two-sided exponential $3e^{-2|\tau|}$ is valid: it is a telegraph-signal autocorrelation.

steps.prompt: A WSS noise $X(t)$ with $R_X(\tau) = {{P}}\,e^{-|\tau|/\tau_c}$ V² ($\tau_c$ = {{tc|s}}) reaches a receiver directly and through an echo delayed by $T_0$ = {{T0|s}}: $Y(t) = X(t) + X(t - T_0)$. What is the average power of $Y$, in V²?
steps.explanation: $E[Y^2] = E[X^2(t)] + E[X^2(t-T_0)] + 2E[X(t)X(t-T_0)] = 2R_X(0) + 2R_X(T_0)$ = 2 × {{P}} + 2 × {{P*exp(-T0/tc)}} = **{{2*P+2*P*exp(-T0/tc)}}** V². For $T_0 \gg \tau_c$ the copies are uncorrelated and the powers simply add ({{2*P}} V²); for $T_0 \ll \tau_c$ they add coherently ({{4*P}} V²).

steps.prompt: Packets arrive as a Poisson process at {{lam}} per second, and a packet has just arrived. What is the probability that the next one takes more than {{t|s}}? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: Interarrival times of a Poisson process are exponential with rate λ: $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$ = $e^{-{{lam*t}}}$ = **{{exp(-lam*t)}}**. (Equivalently: no arrival in an interval of length $t$.)

steps.prompt: A noise process is WSS and ergodic. Put the steps for measuring its autocorrelation $R_X(\tau)$ from a recording in order.
items: Repeat for other delays $\tau$ to trace out $R_X(\tau)$
steps.explanation: Ergodicity lets one long record replace the ensemble: the time average of $x(t)\,x(t+\tau)$ converges to $E[X(t)X(t+\tau)] = R_X(\tau)$. Delay, multiply and average is exactly what a correlator does, once for every $\tau$ of interest. For a non-ergodic process (such as a random constant offset) the result would only describe the one sample function that was recorded.

steps.prompt: A received signal is $X(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_0t + \Theta) + N(t)$ with $A$ = {{A|V}}, $f_0$ = 1 kHz, Θ uniform, and independent zero-mean noise with $R_N(\tau) = {{s2}}\,e^{-|\tau|/\tau_c}$ V², $\tau_c$ = {{tc|s}}.

ask.prompt: What is the signal-to-noise ratio (power) in dB?
What is $R_X(\tau)$ at $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}, in V²?
ask.explanation: The cross terms vanish (independent, zero mean), so $R_X(\tau) = \frac{A^2}{2}\cos(2\pi f_0\tau) + R_N(\tau)$. At τ = {{tau|s}} ≫ τc the noise term is negligible, leaving {{A^2/2}} × ({{cos(2*pi*1000*tau)}}) = **{{A^2/2*cos(2*pi*1000*tau)}}** V². The autocorrelation reveals the sinusoid even though the SNR is only {{10*log10(A^2/2/s2)||2}} dB.

steps.prompt: A BPSK-like signal $Y(t) = X(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct + \Theta)$ multiplies a random binary wave $X(t)$ of ±{{A|V}} at 1 Mbit/s with a 10 MHz carrier of random phase Θ (independent of $X$). What is $R_Y(\tau)$ at τ = {{tau|s}}, in V²?
steps.explanation: Independence lets the expectation factor: $R_Y(\tau) = R_X(\tau)\cdot\frac12\cos(2\pi f_c\tau)$. Here $\tau/T$ = {{fr}}, so $R_X(\tau) = A^2(1 - |\tau|/T)$ = {{A^2*(1-fr)}} V², and ½cos(2π × 10 MHz × {{tau|s}}) = {{0.5*cos(2*pi*1e7*tau)}}. $R_Y$ = **{{A^2*(1-fr)*0.5*cos(2*pi*1e7*tau)}}** V².

steps.prompt: A DC current of {{I|A}} is a Poisson stream of electrons ($q = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C). Count the electrons that pass in a window of {{T|s}}.

ask.prompt: What is the mean number of electrons in the window?
ask.explanation: Rate $\lambda = I/q$, so the mean count is $\lambda T = IT/q$ = {{I|A}} × {{T|s}} / ($1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) = **{{I*T/1.6e-19}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the relative fluctuation $\sigma/\text{mean}$ of the count, in %?
ask.explanation: Poisson: $\sigma = \sqrt{\lambda T}$, so $\sigma/\text{mean} = 1/\sqrt{\lambda T}$ = 1/√{{I*T/1.6e-19}} = **{{100/sqrt(I*T/1.6e-19)}} %**. This is shot noise: small currents measured over short windows fluctuate the most.

steps.prompt: Measurements show that a random telegraph signal has a correlation coefficient of {{c}} between samples {{tau|s}} apart. What is its average switching rate α, in switchings per second?
Set the bit period $T$ of a random binary wave so that samples 1 ms apart have a correlation coefficient of {{c}} (dashed line).
steps.explanation: $\rho(\tau) = 1 - |\tau|/T$ for $|\tau| < T$, so $T = \frac{\tau}{1 - \rho}$ = 1 ms / {{1-c}} = **{{Tt|s}}**, i.e. {{1/Tt}} bit/s.

steps.prompt: $X(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_0t + \Theta)$ with a random amplitude $A$ and an independent uniform phase Θ is ergodic in power: the time-average power of one sample function equals $R_X(0)$.
steps.explanation: $R_X(0) = E[A^2]/2$, but one sample function has time-average power $A^2/2$ for its own amplitude, which differs from one sample function to the next. The process is WSS but not ergodic in power. With a fixed amplitude it would be.

steps.prompt: Packets arrive as a Poisson process at {{lam}} per ms. What is the probability that the count in the first ms is exactly {{k1}} **and** the count in the following 2 ms is exactly {{k2}}? (probability, 0–1)
steps.explanation: Counts in non-overlapping intervals are independent (independent increments), so multiply two Poisson probabilities with means λ × 1 ms = {{lam}} and λ × 2 ms = {{2*lam}}: {{lam^k1*exp(-lam)/fact(k1)}} × {{(2*lam)^k2*exp(-2*lam)/fact(k2)}} = **{{lam^k1*exp(-lam)/fact(k1)*(2*lam)^k2*exp(-2*lam)/fact(k2)}}**.
